explanations.answer: Cross over armed ahead of their brothers
explanations.explanation: Moses, Israel's leader, tells these men, "All your men of valor are to cross over, armed for battle, ahead of your brothers, the Israelites." Their own land is already settled, but their brothers don't have theirs yet. So these men go first. That's like getting your own keys and then being asked to help carry everybody else's couch.

explanations.answer: Stay behind and guard their new cities
explanations.explanation: Close, because somebody does stay in those cities. But it's not the men of valor. Moses says their wives, children and livestock may remain there. The fighting men are told to cross over armed.

explanations.answer: Build a wall along the Jordan River
explanations.explanation: No wall shows up anywhere in this passage, friend. The Jordan is described as a border (Deuteronomy 3:17), and Moses tells the men to cross it. They're going over that river, not fencing it. I'd say building a wall is a lot of work for a river they're about to walk across.

That's not what Moses says. He says the wives, children and livestock "may remain in the cities I have given you." Only the men of valor cross over, armed for battle. The families and herds get to stay put.

That's right. Moses says the wives, children and livestock "may remain in the cities I have given you." Only the men of valor are told to cross over armed. Everybody else stays home, and the herds don't have to go anywhere.

Yes. Moses says the families and herds stay "until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as He has to you." These tribes already have rest, and the rest of Israel is still waiting for theirs. The men only cross over until that day comes.
I get it, they do have a lot of livestock. But the word in the verse isn't wealth. Moses says the LORD gives "rest to your brothers as He has to you." Nobody is being handed a bank account here.

Wisdom is a good thing to want, and Moses talks about it elsewhere in this sermon. But in this verse, the families stay "until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as He has to you." The word is rest. The brothers are waiting on land, not on a smarter brain.

explanations.answer: Return to the land Moses gave him
explanations.explanation: Moses says, "Then each of you may return to the possession I have given you." First the brothers take possession of the land the LORD is giving them across the Jordan. After that, these men go home to what they already have. I'd bet the walk home feels pretty good.

explanations.answer: Pick new land on the west side
explanations.explanation: No, friend. The land west of the Jordan is for their brothers, who are waiting to take possession of it. Moses tells these men they may return "to the possession I have given you." They already have their land, so there's nothing to pick.

explanations.answer: Stay on to serve under Joshua
explanations.explanation: Joshua is mentioned in this passage, but not for this. Moses tells these men that once their brothers have their land, each may return to the possession Moses gave him. Joshua is the one the LORD tells Moses to commission and encourage. The men's orders say go home.

explanations.answer: The LORD Himself will fight for him
explanations.explanation: Moses tells Joshua, "Do not be afraid of them, for the LORD your God Himself will fight for you." Joshua is Moses' attendant, and he's the one about to lead Israel into those kingdoms. Moses points him to what Joshua has already seen the LORD do to the two kings. So the reason isn't how strong Joshua is. It's who is fighting.

explanations.answer: Israel's army is far bigger than theirs
explanations.explanation: Moses never compares the armies, friend. The reason he gives is that "the LORD your God Himself will fight for you." If the plan depended on counting soldiers, Moses would have said something about counting soldiers.

Nothing here says they've surrendered. Moses says these are kingdoms Joshua is "about to enter," and he tells him not to be afraid of them. The reason is that "the LORD your God Himself will fight for you." You don't tell someone not to be afraid of a kingdom that already gave up.

explanations.answer: To cross over and see the good land
explanations.explanation: Moses asks, "Please let me cross over and see the good land beyond the Jordan." He also names the pleasant hill country and Lebanon. He has walked with Israel all this way, and he wants to see the land with them. I think that's a very human thing to want.

explanations.answer: To defeat one more king in battle
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't ask for another battle. Israel has already beaten two kings, Sihon and Og, in this part of the sermon. What Moses asks for is to cross over and see the good land.

explanations.answer: To see the face of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Not here, friend. Moses calls the LORD great and powerful and asks something different: "Please let me cross over and see the good land beyond the Jordan." His request is about the land, not about seeing the LORD's face.
That's the opposite of what the LORD says. He tells Moses, "That is enough… Do not speak to Me again about this matter." Moses doesn't get a later date to ask again. The LORD closes the subject.
That's right. The LORD tells Moses, "That is enough… Do not speak to Me again about this matter." There's no "ask me later" in that. The subject is closed, and Moses is told to stop bringing it up.

explanations.answer: Look over the land in every direction
explanations.explanation: The LORD tells Moses, "Go to the top of Pisgah and look to the west and north and south and east. See the land with your own eyes." That's all four directions. Moses can't walk in, but he can look at all of it. Pisgah is a pretty good place to stand for that.

explanations.answer: Pray for the people camped below
explanations.explanation: Praying is a good thing to do on a mountain. But that isn't the order here. The LORD tells Moses to go to the top of Pisgah and look to the west, north, south and east. He's sent up there to see the land with his own eyes.

explanations.answer: Build an altar out of the stones
explanations.explanation: The LORD says nothing about an altar here, friend. His order for the top of Pisgah is to look to the west, north, south and east. No stones, no building, just Moses and the view.

Yes. The LORD says, "See the land with your own eyes, for you will not cross this Jordan." Moses gets to look but not to walk in. I think that's a heavy thing to hear, and it's okay to let it be heavy.

The text says the opposite. The LORD tells Moses, "See the land with your own eyes, for you will not cross this Jordan." Moses will look at the land from Pisgah but won't go in. I think that one stings.

The LORD says, "But commission Joshua, encourage him, and strengthen him." Moses won't be crossing, but he still has a job to do for the man who will. I think that's a kind way to spend your last stretch. He's handing off the work and cheering on the guy who gets to carry it.

Moses is walking through the whole journey out loud in this sermon, but that's not the order here. The LORD tells him to "commission Joshua, encourage him, and strengthen him." The last order in this passage is about a person, not a notebook.

No tribe blessings in this passage, friend. Moses has just handed out land to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh. But the LORD's last order here is to "commission Joshua, encourage him, and strengthen him."

That's the word. The LORD says Joshua "will cross over ahead of the people and enable them to inherit the land that you will see." Moses is the one who will see the land, and Joshua is the one who leads them into it. Moses sees it, Joshua helps Israel receive it.
Guarding sounds like a fair guess for a leader. But the LORD says Joshua will "enable them to inherit the land that you will see." The word is inherit. It's a gift they receive.
Rebuilding would mean something got knocked down first, and the verse doesn't say that. The LORD says Joshua will "enable them to inherit the land that you will see." The word is inherit.
